title: Two Kingdoms, One King
psalm: Psalm 1 — two ways, two trees, two ends.
action: Walk the trail once this week; choose your notebook; read Psalm 1 aloud each morning.
overview: Two lines run through your Bible. The gold line is a kingdom you could touch — real throne, real crowns, real blood: Saul, David, Solomon, all the way to a Cross. The blue line is a Kingdom you could never vote out: God ruling by His Spirit and His Word. They run parallel, they never cancel each other, and at the very end God marries them — twelve gates named for the tribes, twelve foundations named for the apostles (Revelation 21:12-14). This week opens the whole map.

sections.h: Why this parable first
sections.t: Jesus Himself ranked it: “Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?” (Mark 4:13). The Sower is not one parable among many — it is the interpretive key Jesus hands us before He opens the rest of the Kingdom's mysteries. That is why this series begins here, and why the website you are reading begins here too.

sections.h: The Bible foundation — the text itself
sections.t: Read Matthew 13:3-9 slowly, then let Jesus interpret His own story in Matthew 13:18-23. Three witnesses carry the parable across the Gospels: Matthew 13, Mark 4:3-20, and Luke 8:4-15 — and Luke adds the definition the whole series stands on: “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11). The Kingdom does not arrive by force or argument; it arrives by seed — the Word, received. Peter presses the same image to its full depth: we are “born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the word of God” (1 Peter 1:23). The seed does not merely inform you. It regenerates you.

sections.h: Four soils — one Sower
sections.t: The wayside hearer loses the seed to the birds before it enters — “then cometh the devil, and taketh away the word out of their hearts” (Luke 8:12): the enemy's first move is always against the seed. The stony hearer receives with joy and dies in the heat because there is no root — emotion without depth. The thorny hearer is the modern West's portrait and maybe Kinshasa's too: “the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word” (Matthew 13:22). And the good ground? Luke's wording is precious: “an honest and good heart” that hears, keeps, and brings forth fruit with patience (Luke 8:15). Notice what distinguishes the soils — never the seed, never the Sower. Only reception.

sections.h: What the Message adds
sections.t: The Message presses the parable one step further than most pulpits do. If the seed is the Word, then the Word behaves like a seed: it carries a life inside it, it reproduces only its own kind, and it must go into the ground and die before it multiplies. Genesis says every seed brings forth after its kind; Jesus says the good seed are the children of the Kingdom; Peter says we are born again of incorruptible seed, by the Word of God. Put those together and the parable stops being a story about four kinds of people and becomes a story about one kind of life — God's — trying to reproduce itself in human hearts. That is why the Message insists on the original seed: an idea about God, a tradition about God, a creed about God can be sown and can even sprout, but it cannot produce God's life, because the life is only in the Word He actually spoke. The four soils, then, are four ways a heart receives that seed in every generation, not just in Galilee. And the harvest is not moral improvement; it is the character of Christ, the seed-Word grown up, in a believer. The Bible's own point lands here: the Sower did not fail, the seed did not fail — the only question the parable leaves open is the ground. Hear the Word, keep it, and let it grow with patience; that, Jesus says, is good ground.

sections.h: Outside sources — the world Jesus drew from
sections.t: First-century Galilean farmers sowed broadcast-style before plowing — seed really did land on paths, rock-shelves and thorn patches; Jesus' audience had watched this every autumn. The parable is not agricultural fantasy but photographic realism, which is exactly the point: the Kingdom hides inside ordinary reality until you have ears to hear.
sections.src: Joachim Jeremias, The Parables of Jesus (rev. ed. 1972) · Jubilees 11:11 · Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 73b · Philip B. Payne, “The Order of Sowing and Ploughing in the Parable of the Sower,” New Testament Studies 25 (1978) · Kenneth E. Bailey, Jesus Through Middle Eastern Eyes (2008)

sections.h: For your life this week
sections.t: The most contested territory on earth is about four inches wide and sits behind your ribs. This week Israel will ask for a king and hear God say “they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me” (1 Samuel 8:7) — a nation's soil test. Yours runs at the same time. Which soil are you, honestly, this season? The good news of the parable is that soil is not fate: paths can be broken up, stones can be cleared, thorns can be pulled. “Break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD” (Hosea 10:12).

sections.h: What remains open
sections.t: Interpreters differ on whether the birds, measurements of fruit (thirty, sixty, hundredfold) and the field's scope carry fixed prophetic identifications. We hold the text's own interpretation as controlling and mark everything beyond it as teaching comparison, not doctrine.

trackA.title: The Road to the Cross
trackA.t: The earthly line opens at Shiloh and Ramah: a theocracy exhausted by corrupt priests, a praying mother, a boy who learned to say “Speak; for thy servant heareth” (1 Samuel 3:10). This week is the flyover: Israel demands a visible king (1 Samuel 8), God grants Saul, chooses David, swears the covenant (2 Samuel 7:16), lets glory rise under Solomon and split under his son; prophets plead, Assyria takes the north, Babylon burns the house; Daniel reads the empires; a remnant returns; four hundred years go silent — and then a Man rides into Jerusalem on a colt while crowds sing Psalm 118, and the line runs straight into a Cross bearing a royal charge: THE KING OF THE JEWS. Blood history, running TO the Cross. Archaeology even carries the dynasty's name — “House of David,” cut in stone by Israel's enemies at Tel Dan.

sections.h: Where the gold line starts: a lamp nearly out at Shiloh
sections.t: Before Israel had a king it had a tent. For roughly three centuries after Joshua the tabernacle stood at Shiloh in the hill country of Ephraim (Joshua 18:1; Judges 21:19), and the nation was a theocracy — no palace, no standing army, no capital; God ruling by His Word through priests and judges. By the opening of 1 Samuel that arrangement was rotting from the top. Eli's sons “were sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD” (1 Samuel 2:12); they took the meat of the offerings by force and lay with the women at the tabernacle door (2:16, 22); and “the word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision” (3:1). Into that silence God sent a barren woman's prayer. Hannah's vow (1:11), Hannah's song (2:1-10) — which ends, astonishingly, with the first mention of a king and an anointed one in the whole book: “he shall give strength unto his king, and exalt the horn of his anointed” (2:10) — and Hannah's son Samuel, the last of the judges and the first of the kingmakers. The boy learned to say “Speak; for thy servant heareth” (3:10) while “the lamp of God went out in the temple of the LORD” (3:3). That is the soil the gold line grows from: a corrupt priesthood, a praying mother, and a child who could hear.

sections.h: The world around Shiloh
sections.src: Israel Finkelstein, Shlomo Bunimovitz and Zvi Lederman, Shiloh: The Archaeology of a Biblical Site (Tel Aviv University, 1993) · Trude Dothan, The Philistines and Their Material Culture (1982) · K. A. Kitchen, On the Reliability of the Old Testament (2003) · William Day Crockett, A Harmony of the Books of Samuel, Kings and Chronicles (Revell, 1897), Book I “Until the Monarchy”
sections.t: Shiloh is a real hill, Khirbet Seilun, about thirty kilometres north of Jerusalem. Excavation there has exposed storerooms from Samuel's period packed with the big collared-rim jars Israelite villagers kept their grain and oil in — and a thick layer of burnt destruction from the same era. The Bible never narrates Shiloh's fall; it only assumes it, when Jeremiah tells Jerusalem to go and look at what God did to Shiloh (Jeremiah 7:12; 26:6; Psalm 78:60). The ground and the text agree. Israel in this period was a loose federation of hill-country villages — small four-room houses, terraced slopes, no monumental building, almost no writing — squeezed between the Canaanite valleys and the Philistine cities of the coastal plain. The Philistines were part of the “Sea Peoples” who settled that coast a generation or two before Samuel; they had five lords over five fortified cities (Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath) and, critically, a monopoly on ironwork: “there was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel: for the Philistines said, Lest the Hebrews make them swords or spears” (1 Samuel 13:19). Israel's cry for a king “like all the nations” (8:5, 20) was made under that military pressure — which does not excuse it, but explains it. The old harmony of Samuel, Kings and Chronicles that we follow files this whole stretch under one heading: the story before there was a story of kings.

sections.h: Give us a king — the demand and the mirror
sections.t: The gold line proper begins with a rejection. When Samuel was old and his own sons took bribes at Beersheba (1 Samuel 8:3), the elders asked for a king “to judge us like all the nations” (8:5). God's verdict is the hinge of this whole series: “they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them” (8:7). He had anticipated the request centuries earlier — Deuteronomy 17:14-20 already lays down the manner of a king who must not multiply horses, wives or silver, and who must copy the Law out with his own hand — so kingship itself was not the sin; the motive was. Samuel warns them what “the manner of the king” will cost (8:11-18): their sons, their daughters, their fields, a tenth of everything, and finally their freedom — “and ye shall cry out in that day because of your king… and the LORD will not hear you.” They answered, “Nay; but we will have a king over us” (8:19). So God gave them Saul: a head taller than anyone (9:2; 10:23), from the smallest tribe, hiding among the baggage on coronation day (10:22) — a tall king for a shallow demand. Saul's reign is the study of a man who had the Spirit (10:10; 11:6) and lost the throne through impatience at Gilgal (13:8-14) and partial obedience over Amalek (15:22-23): “to obey is better than sacrifice… Because thou hast rejected the word of the LORD, he hath also rejected thee from being king.” The very word Israel used on God in chapter eight comes back on Saul in chapter fifteen. The kingdom is torn from him like the hem of Samuel's robe (15:27-28) — “and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou.”

sections.h: The shepherd from Bethlehem — and the throne that was sworn
sections.t: “The LORD seeth not as man seeth… the LORD looketh on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). While Saul still wore the crown, Samuel poured oil on the youngest son of Jesse in Bethlehem, “and the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward” (16:13). Everything that follows on the gold line is the story of an anointed king who has not yet been enthroned: Goliath's valley and “the battle is the LORD's” (17:47); Saul's javelin; Jonathan's covenant; the cave of Adullam, where “every one that was in distress, and every one that was in debt, and every one that was discontented, gathered themselves unto him” (22:2); the years of sparing the king he could have killed (24; 26). Then Gilboa, Hebron, Jerusalem, the ark brought up with dancing (2 Samuel 6) — and the night God swore the oath that holds the entire line together: “thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee: thy throne shall be established for ever” (2 Samuel 7:16). Psalm 89 calls it a covenant sworn by God's own holiness: “I will not lie unto David” (89:35). From there the road runs through Solomon's glory and Solomon's fall; the split at Shechem into two houses (1 Kings 12); nineteen kings in the north, not one of them good, until Samaria fell to Assyria; twenty in the south, some of them good, until Babylon burned the house and put out the eyes of the last king of David's line (2 Kings 25:7). Daniel read the empires from inside the captivity; a remnant came home under Cyrus; the prophets fell silent for four centuries — and then the genealogies of Matthew 1 and Luke 3 deliver the Seed. A Man rides into Jerusalem on a colt while the crowd sings Psalm 118, and Pilate nails the line's whole claim over His head in three languages: THE KING OF THE JEWS (John 19:19). The road to the Cross is a road of blood, crowns and failure that God never once let go of.

sections.h: Receipts from the ground
sections.src: Avraham Biran and Joseph Naveh, “An Aramaic Stele Fragment from Tel Dan,” Israel Exploration Journal 43 (1993) and 45 (1995) · the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III, the Taylor Prism of Sennacherib and the Lachish reliefs (British Museum) · Babylonian Chronicle BM 21946 (British Museum) · the Cyrus Cylinder (British Museum) · Edwin R. Thiele, The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings (3rd ed., 1983) · Merrill, A Harmony of the Kings and Prophets (Massachusetts Sabbath School Society, 1832) · K. A. Kitchen, On the Reliability of the Old Testament (2003)
sections.t: For most of the last two centuries the critics said David was a legend. Then, in the summer of 1993 at Tel Dan in the far north of Israel, an Aramaic victory inscription came out of a wall — set up by a king of Damascus boasting that he had killed a “king of Israel” and a king of “the House of David.” Israel's enemies, carving the dynasty's name in stone roughly a hundred and thirty years after David died. It stands today in the Israel Museum. And it is not alone. The Black Obelisk from Nimrud shows Jehu of Israel — or his envoy — on his face before Shalmaneser III of Assyria: the only picture of an Israelite king ever found. Sennacherib's own prism describes shutting Hezekiah up in Jerusalem “like a bird in a cage” and, tellingly, never claims to have taken the city (2 Kings 19:35-36). The Lachish reliefs from Nineveh show in stone the siege the Bible gives one line (2 Kings 18:14). A Babylonian chronicle tablet records Nebuchadnezzar taking Jerusalem and installing a king of his own choosing; the Cyrus Cylinder records the Persian policy of sending captive peoples home with their gods — the policy behind Ezra 1. The Bible's kings also lock into datable Assyrian and Babylonian records, which is how we can say when the kingdom divided (about 931 BC), when Samaria fell (722/721) and when Jerusalem burned (587/586). The older harmony we also use carries slightly different, traditional dates; where they differ we teach the anchored date first and show the older one in parentheses.

sections.h: What the Message says about the earthly throne
sections.t: The earthly kingdom was never the point; it was the picture. God works the same way every time — first the natural, then the spiritual: a natural Israel before a spiritual one, a natural birth before the new birth, a throne of stone in Jerusalem before the throne it was always pointing at. The Message keeps the two kingdoms clearly apart and then shows how they belong to each other. Israel asked for a king they could see because they had stopped being able to hear the King they could not see; that is why the demand of 1 Samuel 8 is a heart problem before it is a political one — the same problem the Sower diagnoses, seed refused by the ground. God answered the demand twice. Saul was the people's choice, everything a nation wants in a king, and he came apart under pressure. David was God's choice, taken from behind the sheep, and he is the pattern of the King who was coming: anointed long before he was crowned, rejected by the ruling house, hunted, gathering a company of the distressed and the indebted and the discontented in a cave while the wrong man sat on the throne. That is exactly where the Church stands now — with an anointed King who has not yet taken His visible seat, and a company that has gone out to Him, outside the camp. The covenant with David is taken literally: the throne is a real throne, the house is a real house, and the Son of David will sit on it in Jerusalem when He returns — the promise is not spiritualised away, it is waiting for the King to come back. That is why the gold line runs through failure after failure without breaking: it does not rest on the men who sat on the throne, it rests on an oath God swore by Himself. And when the line reaches the Cross, the sign over His head is not an insult the Bible is embarrassed by; it is the title deed. The King of the Jews died with His claim written above Him, and every crown on the gold line was only ever a rehearsal for that one.

sections.h: What remains open on this road
sections.t: Three things we hold loosely. First, the numbers: the traditional harmony dates and the modern anchored dates differ by about forty years at the split of the kingdom and by only a couple by Josiah — we teach the anchored dates, show the older ones, and hang no doctrine on either. Second, the size of David's kingdom: some archaeologists read the tenth-century remains as a small chiefdom, others as the state the Bible describes; the fortified town at Khirbet Qeiyafa and the “House of David” stone have moved that argument, but it is still an argument, and we report it as one. Third, the length of Saul's reign: the Hebrew of 1 Samuel 13:1 has lost a number, and Acts 13:21 supplies forty years — we go with Acts and say so. None of this touches the oath of 2 Samuel 7. It is the scaffolding, not the building.

trackB.title: The Road from the Cross
trackB.t: The spiritual line is older than any crown — it begins wherever someone believes God: Abel's altar, Enoch's walk, Abraham's “he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). It runs quiet under the whole Old Testament in the mouths of prophets — God ruling by His Word while thrones drift. At the Cross it ignites: the veil rips (Matthew 27:51), the Spirit falls at Pentecost, and Peter's first sermon plants the flag on a Davidic text — God “would raise up Christ to sit on his throne” (Acts 2:30). From there: the apostolic church, seven lampstands, a Bride being made ready, a catching away, a Wedding Supper, a return WITH the King, and a City whose gates and foundations finally marry the two histories. Spirit history, running FROM the Cross.

sections.h: A Kingdom older than any crown
sections.t: The blue line does not start at Pentecost; it starts at Eden's gate. The first promise in the Bible is not about a throne but about a Seed — the woman's Seed who would bruise the serpent's head (Genesis 3:15) — and the first two brothers show the two ways that promise can be received: Cain brought the work of his hands, Abel brought blood, “and the LORD had respect unto Abel and to his offering” (Genesis 4:4; Hebrews 11:4). From there it runs through Enoch, who “walked with God: and he was not; for God took him” (Genesis 5:24) — the first man caught away, a picture the line will come back to; through Noah, who “moved with fear, prepared an ark” (Hebrews 11:7); through Abram, who “believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness” (Genesis 15:6) — four hundred and thirty years before the Law and long before any throne (Galatians 3:17). The line even has its own king in the middle of Genesis: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the most high God, who brings out bread and wine and blesses Abram (Genesis 14:18-20). Psalm 110 makes him the pattern of the Messiah's priesthood, and Hebrews 7 spends a whole chapter on why — a King-Priest with no genealogy and no beginning of days: the heavenly Kingdom stepping into the earthly story for one meal. This is the Kingdom Jesus meant when He said it “cometh not with observation… the kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:20-21): God reigning in hearts by His Word, before Saul, before David, before Rome.

sections.h: The Bride hidden in the Old Testament
sections.t: The blue line carries a name the gold line never uses: Bride. It is sown quietly and early. Adam is put to sleep and a bride is taken from his side (Genesis 2:21-24), and Paul says plainly that this “great mystery” is about Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31-32). Abraham sends his servant to fetch a bride for his son from his own kindred; the servant will not eat until he has spoken, and Rebekah says “I will go” before she has ever seen Isaac (Genesis 24) — a servant sent to win a bride for a son she has not seen; the Church knows that story from the inside (1 Peter 1:8). Joseph, rejected by his brothers, takes a Gentile bride during his exile and is revealed to Israel afterwards (Genesis 41:45; 45:1). And in Bethlehem — the town of the gold line — a Moabite widow gleans in the field of Boaz, a kinsman with the right to redeem, and in one night on a threshing floor the two lines touch: Ruth the Gentile bride becomes the great-grandmother of David (Ruth 4:13-22). The prophets say it out loud. “Thy Maker is thine husband” (Isaiah 54:5). “I will betroth thee unto me for ever” (Hosea 2:19). Psalm 45, a wedding song for a king, tells the bride to “forget also thine own people, and thy father's house” (45:10) — and Hebrews 1 quotes the same psalm about the Son. The Song of Songs sings the whole relationship. When John the Baptist called himself “the friend of the bridegroom” (John 3:29), he was not inventing an image; he was finishing one.

sections.h: The Cross — where the blue line catches fire
sections.t: At the ninth hour of a Friday outside Jerusalem the two lines met. The gold line delivered its King to a Roman cross with His title nailed above Him; and at the moment He gave up the ghost, “the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom” (Matthew 27:51) — torn from God's side, not man's. Fifty days later, on the feast of Pentecost, the Spirit fell on about a hundred and twenty in an upper room “as of a rushing mighty wind,” with “cloven tongues like as of fire” (Acts 2:2-3), and Peter's first sermon stood on a Davidic text: God had sworn to David “that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne” (Acts 2:30), and the resurrection was the proof. About three thousand were added that day. This is the birthday of the Church, the called-out company, and from her first sermon her Kingdom was understood as the continuation of David's — James says the same at the Jerusalem council: “I will build again the tabernacle of David, which is fallen down” (Acts 15:16). Paul later put the whole blue line into one sentence: “I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2) — and in the same breath warned that the serpent who beguiled Eve would try to corrupt her too (11:3). The seed of the Sower is the Word; the Bride is what the Word grows into when a heart receives it.

sections.h: The world the Church was born into
sections.src: Tacitus, Annals 15.44 · Pliny the Younger, Letters 10.96–97 · Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 18.3.3, 18.5.2 and 20.9.1 · F. F. Bruce, The Spreading Flame (1958) and The New Testament Documents: Are They Reliable? (1943) · Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church, vol. 1 (1882)
sections.t: Pentecost drew pilgrims “out of every nation under heaven” (Acts 2:5) — Parthians, Medes, Elamites, Mesopotamia, Judaea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, Libya, Rome, Cretans and Arabians (2:9-11) — because the Jewish dispersion by then reached from Babylon to Spain, with a synagogue in almost every city. That network became the Church's road system: wherever Paul went, he began in the synagogue. Rome supplied the rest — paved roads, a policed sea, one common Greek across the eastern Mediterranean — so that a letter written in Corinth could be read in Rome within weeks. The empire noticed the new movement and did not like it. Tacitus, writing about the great fire under Nero, records that “Christus” had been executed by Pontius Pilate in the reign of Tiberius, and that the “superstition” had broken out again in Judaea and reached the capital. Pliny, governing Bithynia, wrote to the emperor Trajan asking what to do with Christians who met before dawn to sing to Christ “as to a god,” bound themselves by oath not to steal or commit adultery — and would not curse Christ even to save their lives. Josephus, a Jewish historian working in Rome, knew of Jesus, of John the Baptist's execution, and of James “the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ.” None of these men were believers. That is the point: the blue line leaves footprints in the records of the people who tried to stamp it out.

sections.h: Seven lampstands to a City
sections.t: The last book of the Bible is the blue line's map. John, exiled on Patmos, sees the risen King walking among seven golden lampstands — “the seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches” (Revelation 1:20) — and dictates seven letters to seven real congregations in Asia that also read, in order, like the whole history of the Church from the apostles to the end. Then a door opens in heaven and a voice says “Come up hither” (4:1), and from that point the Church is seen in heaven, not on earth: elders around the throne, a Lamb opening a sealed book, a woman clothed with the sun, a multitude no man can number. Near the end the language turns to a wedding: “the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready” (19:7), dressed in “the righteousness of saints,” and the King rides out of heaven with the armies that follow Him (19:11-14). Then a thousand years, a judgment, and the last picture in the Bible: “the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (21:2). The angel who shows John the city calls it “the bride, the Lamb's wife” (21:9) — a city that is a people. And on that city God has written both histories: the names of the twelve tribes on the gates, the names of the twelve apostles on the foundations (21:12-14). The gold line and the blue line do not dissolve into one another. They are married — and the architecture is the certificate.

sections.h: What the Message says about the Bride
sections.t: The Bride is the Word made flesh in a people. That is the one sentence to carry out of this week. The seed of the parable is the Word; the Bride is that seed grown to full stature — a company that has received the original Word, kept it, and become what it says, the way a wheat seed becomes wheat and nothing else. The Message draws a line the Bible itself draws: the church is the called-out — many are called — but the Bride is the chosen, and few are chosen. She was chosen in Him before the foundation of the world, so her story cannot begin at Pentecost or with any organisation; it begins in the mind of God, and it surfaces wherever a heart believes what God actually said, from Abel's altar onward. The seven churches of Revelation are read as seven ages of that story, each with its own portion of light and its own messenger, and the pattern across them is a Word lost by degrees and restored by degrees — until the last age, where the full Word is given back to a Bride so that she can be caught up to meet the King, the way Enoch was taken and the way the door opened for John. That catching away comes before the trouble, not after it, and it is what turns the gold line back on: once the Bride is gone, Israel steps back into the story to receive her King. The two Lines run side by side the entire way and marry at the City, and nobody gets to skip a line. A Word-Bride does not need a crown to be royal, and she will not settle for a creed when she can have the Seed. She is being made ready now — which is what a study like this is for.

sections.h: What remains open on this road
sections.t: Believers who love the same Bible read the timing of the catching away differently — before, in the middle of, or after the time of trouble — and read the seven churches either as seven congregations only or as seven periods as well. We teach the view above as our working map and say so plainly, while holding John's text as the thing that governs the map and not the other way round. And where we say “the Bride” and “the church,” we mean a distinction the Bible itself makes — many called, few chosen — not a label for anyone's membership roll, including ours.

storyA: Before there was a throne in Israel there was a lamp in Shiloh, nearly gone out. The priest's sons stole from the offerings; the people drifted; and a barren woman named Hannah wept her way into history — because the answer to a corrupt priesthood was not a committee, it was a baby dedicated to God. Samuel grew up hearing what Eli could no longer hear. And when Israel finally shouted for a king “like all the nations,” God let them have their mirror — a tall king for a shallow demand — while already looking toward Bethlehem, where a shepherd boy was learning to kill lions in secret. The road to the Cross begins here: with a nation trading the invisible King for a visible one, and God, in mercy, planning to give them a King who was both.
storyB: The second road does not begin at a coronation — it begins at an altar outside Eden, where Abel brought blood and was heard. It runs through Enoch, who walked instead of marched; through Noah, who built instead of argued; through Abram, who believed God in the dark and was counted righteous before he was circumcised, before the Law, before the throne. This is the Kingdom that never needed a palace: God ruling hearts by His Word. All through Israel's royal centuries this quiet line runs beneath the loud one — prophets over kings, altars over armies — waiting for the night when the two roads would touch at a wooden crossbeam outside Jerusalem, and the quiet one would catch fire.

What did God swear to David in 2 Samuel 7:16?
opts: That his house, kingdom and throne would be established for ever
That Israel would never be divided
That the temple would stand for ever

quiz.q: What did the Tel Dan Stele give the world?
opts: The words “House of David,” carved by Israel’s enemies

quiz.q: Where does the blue line begin?
opts: At Eden’s gate — the promise of the Seed and Abel’s altar

quiz.q: Who was counted righteous for believing God, long before the Law and any throne?
Which Bethlehem story shows the two lines touching — a Gentile bride who became David’s great-grandmother?
What promise to David did Peter preach at Pentecost (Acts 2:30)?
opts: That the temple would be rebuilt
That God would raise up Christ to sit on David’s throne
That the twelve tribes would return

quiz.q: Whose names are on the City’s gates — and whose on its foundations?
opts: The twelve tribes / the twelve apostles

flash.b: Kingdom — not first a territory but a reign: the right and the act of ruling. “The kingdom of God is within you” means His rule inside, not a country outside.
Seed, the thing sown. “The seed is the word of God” — the Word carries a life inside it and reproduces after its kind.
A sowing; seed that begets. Peter’s word for the incorruptible seed we are born again by.
Seed, offspring — the same word for a farmer’s grain and for a family line. “The good seed are the children of the kingdom.”
Word — a thought expressed; the message with the mind of God behind it. Luke’s word for the seed.
Incorruptible, imperishable — cannot rot. The seed we are born of cannot decay, so neither can what it produces.
To beget again; to be born anew. Not a repair of the old life but a second birth from a second seed.
A mystery — not a puzzle but a secret kept until God chooses to reveal it. “It is given unto you to know the mysteries of the kingdom.”
Heart — the whole inner person: mind, will, affections. The soil in every telling of the parable.
“Honest and good.” Kalos is good as in noble, beautiful, fit for purpose; agathos is good as in beneficial, fruitful. Luke uses both for the good ground.
Patience — staying under a load; endurance. Fruit comes “with patience”: good ground is measured in seasons, not moments.
Church — the called-out assembly. The word says what she is: called out of somewhere, to Someone.
Chosen, elect. “Many are called, but few are chosen” — the Bible’s own line between the called-out and the Bride.
Bride. John’s last name for the Church: “the bride, the Lamb’s wife” — a city that is a people.
Gate · foundation. Twelve gates carry the tribes’ names, twelve foundations carry the apostles’ — both histories built into one City.
To hear — and in Hebrew, to hear is to obey. “Speak; for thy servant heareth” and “to obey is better than sacrifice” use the same word.
To reject, to despise, to refuse. Israel used it on God; God used it on Saul.
To reign, to be king. “That I should not reign over them” — the thing Israel actually refused.
To anoint · the anointed one. Oil poured on a head at God’s order — David was mashiach long before he was king. Christos is the Greek.
Covenant — a binding oath, cut in blood. God’s covenant with David is sworn, not negotiated.

flash.f: bayith · H1004 · mamlakah · H4467 · kisse · H3678
flash.b: House · kingdom · throne — the three things God established “for ever” in one verse. House here means dynasty, not a building — and olam (H5769), “for ever,” runs to the vanishing point.
To believe (to lean your whole weight on) · righteousness. “He believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness” — the blue line’s first formula.
To redeem as a kinsman — to buy back what a relative lost. Boaz’s part for Ruth; Christ’s for the Bride.
Two entries, one spelling: the town where the tabernacle stood, and the title in Jacob’s blessing — “the sceptre shall not depart from Judah… until Shiloh come.”
Barren wife of Elkanah; prayed at Shiloh; her song is the first place 1 Samuel mentions a king and an anointed. Mother of Samuel.
High priest and judge at Shiloh; honoured his sons above God; died hearing that the ark was taken.
Last of the judges, first of the kingmakers; anointed both Saul and David; heard God as a boy while the lamp was going out.
Israel’s first king — the people’s choice: tall, from Benjamin, hiding among the baggage; lost the throne by partial obedience.
Shepherd of Bethlehem, God’s choice; anointed years before he was crowned; received the oath of an everlasting throne.
King of Salem and priest of the most high God; bread and wine for Abram; the pattern of Christ’s priesthood.
The blue line before any throne: blood accepted, a walk with God, an ark built by faith, righteousness counted for believing.
A Moabite widow and a kinsman-redeemer in Bethlehem; the Gentile bride who became David’s great-grandmother — where the two lines touch.
Preached the first sermon of the Church on a promise to David: Christ raised up to sit on his throne.
Hill town in Ephraim where the tabernacle stood for about three centuries; burned in Samuel’s day; Jeremiah used its ruin as a warning.
Sea-people settlers of the coast; five lords, five cities; an iron monopoly — “no smith found throughout all the land of Israel.”
Aramaic victory inscription found in 1993 that names the “House of David” — the dynasty’s name carved by its enemies. Israel Museum.
Assyrian monument from Nimrud showing Jehu of Israel bowing to Shalmaneser III — the only picture of an Israelite king ever found. British Museum.
Three writers of the Roman world, none of them believers, who record Christ’s execution under Pilate, Christians singing to Christ as to a god, and James the brother of Jesus.
“Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?”
“The seed is the word of God.”
“They have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.”
“Thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee: thy throne shall be established for ever.”
“God had sworn with an oath to him, that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne.”
“Howbeit that was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural; and afterward that which is spiritual.”
Jean-François Millet, 1850, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston. A peasant broadcasting seed by hand — the motion Jesus’ hearers had watched every autumn.
Rembrandt, about 1651–1658, Mauritshuis. The king with the spear behind the curtain; the shepherd with the harp.

flash.f: The House of David, in stone
flash.b: The Tel Dan Stele, Israel Museum. Aramaic, carved by a king of Damascus.
The Black Obelisk, British Museum. An Israelite king on his face before Assyria.
Jean II Restout, 1732, Louvre. The rushing wind and the tongues of fire.
The kingdoms of Israel (north) and Judah (south) after the split.

poll.q: Which soil are you, honestly, this season?
opts: The stones — quick joy, shallow root

images.title: The Sower
images.note: Oil on canvas. A peasant broadcasting seed by hand on a hillside at dusk — the exact motion the crowd on the shore of Galilee had watched every autumn.
images.source: Museum of Fine Arts, Boston · via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: The Sower
images.note: Van Gogh painted the sower more than thirty times, following Millet. Here the sun sits behind the sower like a halo; the seed goes into a field the colour of night.
images.source: Kröller-Müller Museum, Otterlo · via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: The Sower (Le semeur)
images.note: Watercolour painted after Tissot’s journeys through Palestine — he drew the fields and the farmers he actually saw.

images.title: Shiloh — the site
images.note: Khirbet Seilun in the hills of Ephraim, where the tabernacle stood for about three centuries and where Hannah prayed. Its burnt layer is still in the ground.

images.title: The High Priest and Hannah
images.note: 1 Samuel 1:12 — Eli watches Hannah’s lips move and thinks she is drunk. A drawing from Tissot’s Old Testament series.
images.source: The Jewish Museum, New York · via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Samuel Blesses Saul
images.note: Engraving from Doré’s illustrated Bible. The old prophet, the tall young man, and the oil that made him king.
images.source: La Grande Bible de Tours · via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: Saul and David
images.note: The king wipes his eye with the curtain, the spear in his other hand; the shepherd plays on, not looking up. Rembrandt painted the whole of 1 Samuel 18 in one gesture.
images.source: Mauritshuis, The Hague · via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: David Slays Goliath
images.note: The valley of Elah. “The battle is the LORD’s” (1 Samuel 17:47).
images.source: La Grande Bible de Tours · via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: The Tel Dan Stele
images.note: Basalt fragments of an Aramaic victory inscription from Dan. Line 9 reads bytdwd — “House of David.” The dynasty’s name, carved by its enemies.
images.source: Israel Museum, Jerusalem · via Wikimedia Commons

images.title: The Black Obelisk — Jehu before Shalmaneser III
images.artist: Photograph by Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin
images.note: Second register, side A: “Jehu, son of Omri” — or his envoy — bows to the ground before the Assyrian king. The only picture of an Israelite king ever found.

images.title: Two houses — Israel and Judah
images.note: After the split at Shechem: ten tribes in the north with Samaria, Judah and Benjamin in the south with Jerusalem. Damascus, Moab, Ammon, Edom and Philistia around them.

images.title: Pentecost
images.note: Oil on canvas, painted for the abbey of Saint-Denis. The rushing mighty wind, the tongues of fire, and the Church born in an upper room.
images.source: Musée du Louvre, Paris · via Wikimedia Commons
